title: Choosing type for a long article
metaTitle: Choosing type for a long article
excerpt: Long reading needs a comfortable line length, real line height, and headings you can scan. Keep display type in the title, and set the body for the paragraph.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall. The connected screens fit a piece about how a long article has to hold together as a reading path.
caption: A long page is a path the eye has to follow. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What type choices matter most in a long article?
faqs.answer: Measure, line height, and headings. The line should be short enough that the eye finds the next one, tall enough that the lines do not collide, and broken by headings that say what the next passage is about. Display faces belong in the title. The body needs a face you can read for many minutes.

faqs.question: How wide should a line of body text be?
faqs.answer: Keep it near a range a reader can cross in one return, roughly 45 to 75 characters on a desktop column. A full-bleed paragraph across a wide monitor is tiring, and a very narrow column makes the argument feel chopped. On a phone the screen already sets a narrower measure. Check that it does not become a stack of two-word lines when the text size increases.

faqs.question: Should the article use the same font as the logo?
faqs.answer: Often no. A logo face is drawn for a word or two at a large size, while body text is drawn for repetition. Echo the brand in the title and the headings, then set the paragraphs in a text face with a calmer rhythm. The reader should feel one site without deciphering the brand on every line.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A long article is a reading task, not a poster. Good blog typography gives the reader a comfortable measure, a real line height, and headings they can scan. The title can be a display face. The body should be a face that disappears into the sentence.

People will not read every word. Nielsen Norman Group notes that, on the pages they do visit, people have time to read only about a quarter of the text, and that the average visit lasts a little less than a minute. The type system has to make that quarter the right quarter: the title, the headings, and the first lines of each section. The paragraphs still have to be good, because the people who stay will actually read them.

## A measure the eye can cross

The measure is the length of a line. Too long, and the eye loses its place on the return. Too short, and the paragraph breaks into a ragged stack and the argument feels breathless. For a desktop article, set a column that lands near 45 to 75 characters. That is a working range, not a law. Read a real paragraph in the real face and adjust.

Do not let the article run the full width of a large monitor. A marketing site can be wide. A paragraph cannot. Put the prose in a column and let the margins be quiet. Images can break the column when they need to. The text should come back to the same width afterward so the rhythm returns.

On a phone the viewport does the narrowing for you. The risk flips. Padding, a large heading, and a floating share bar can leave a line of three words. Set the side padding so the body still has a decent measure at a normal text size, and again when the reader increases the text size. If the layout overflows sideways, the measure is a fiction. They cannot read a line they have to drag.

An editorial page, the kind of long reading a heritage site such as Thomas Bewick has to support, lives or dies on this column. The subject can be rich. The line still has to be ordinary. Ordinary is a compliment in body text.

## Line height and the space between paragraphs

Line height is the air inside the paragraph. Body text set solid, with lines nearly touching, looks dense in a way that is fine for a caption and wrong for an essay. Give the lines enough room that ascenders and descenders do not collide, and that the eye can track. A little more air is safer than a little less, up to the point where the paragraph falls apart into separate stripes.

Paragraph spacing should be visible and smaller than the space before a heading. Readers use that gap to see the structure. A wall of text with no paragraph space, or with a full blank line that looks like a section break, both fail. Pick one method and keep it. Indenting the first line and also adding a large gap is a double signal. On the web, space between paragraphs is the clearer one.

Avoid justifying the column unless you are ready to control rivers and the last line. Left-aligned text with a ragged right edge is the honest setting for a responsive column. The rag will change as the viewport changes. That is fine. A justified line that stretches a short sentence across the measure is not fine.

Hyphenation can help a narrow phone column. Turn it on with care, in the language of the page, and check that names and product words are not sliced into nonsense. If you cannot review it, leave hyphenation off and accept a slightly rougher rag. A bad break in a company name is more distracting than an uneven edge.

## Headings a person can scan

Headings are how a skimmer builds a map. They should be larger or heavier than the body, and they should say the claim of the section. A heading that is the same size as the body, only in a different color, will be missed. A heading in all caps at a huge size will be admired and not read.

Keep the levels few. A title, a section heading, and sometimes a subheading. If you need a fourth level, the article is probably two articles. The space above a heading should be larger than the space below it, so the heading belongs to the text that follows. A heading orphaned at the bottom of a screen is a layout bug. Keep it with the next paragraph.

Do not center every heading in a long piece. Centered display titles can mark the top of the article. Centered section headings make the eye search for the start of the next line. Left alignment matches the body and makes the scan path a straight line down the column.

The first lines under a heading do the rest. Nielsen's point about the quarter of the text people actually read is a writing constraint and a type constraint. If the heading is vague and the first line is a warm-up, the scannable layer is empty. Put the point in both places. The type can only reveal what the words contain.

## Display type stays in the title

A display face is allowed to be particular. It can have a high contrast stroke, a sharp terminal, a personality you would notice on a cover. Use it for the article title, and maybe for a short pull quote if you truly need one. Do not set paragraphs in it. The details that make a display face memorable are the details that tire a reader at body size.

If the brand has one typeface and it is a text face, you may not need a second. Use weight and size to separate title, heading, and body. A system with two families is enough for almost every company site: one for display, one for text, chosen to sit in the same mood. Three families in one article looks like a template that was never edited.

Italics are for emphasis and for titles of works, not for whole paragraphs of "friendly" asides. Bold is for a rare word the eye should catch, not for every other sentence. If everything is emphasized, nothing is. Links should be recognizable without relying on color alone. An underline is the durable signal, especially in a long text where the reader is moving quickly.

Numerals and punctuation deserve a look. A text face with a badly fitting question mark, or old-style figures that collide with the line height you chose, will nag at every heading that asks a question. Set a sample that includes numbers, quotes, and a long word from your own vocabulary. "PostgreSQL" and "checkout" should not look like accidents.

## The phone, the print, and the dark page

Read the article on a phone in the same column width you will ship. Desktop mockups hide cramped lines and headings that wrap into four lines. A heading that wraps is fine. A heading that wraps because the size is theatrical is not. Reduce the size until the heading is two lines at most on a phone, for a normal title. Save the drama for the one title at the top.

If you offer a dark page, do not simply invert a light palette. Thin strokes that looked elegant in black on white can shimmer in white on black. Increase the weight slightly for the dark body, and check the muted color you use for secondary text. Muted does not mean faint. Captions and metadata still have to be readable.

Printing is a useful test even if you expect no one to print. A print stylesheet that drops the navigation and sets the column in a text face will show you whether the article is actually an article. If it only makes sense as a sequence of animated cards, you have designed a brochure, not a piece someone can finish.

Images inside the article need a relationship to the column. A figure that is always full-bleed, with a caption in a different measure and a different face, breaks the reading. Align the caption to the text column. Keep the caption shorter than the picture's interest. The picture is a pause. The type should make it obvious how to resume.

## A reading test before you publish

Read the piece aloud, or at least with your mouth moving, from the title through the first section. Stumble points are often type points: a line break in the middle of a name, a heading that wraps onto a single short word, a paragraph so wide you lose the thread. Fix the break or the width. Do not only rewrite the sentence to dodge a layout you should have set properly.

Time a cold read of the whole article at a normal pace. If you are exhausted before the argument is done, the line height or the measure is wrong, or the writing is repeating itself. Type will not rescue repetition. It will expose it. Cut the repeated point, then check the type again.

Hand the phone to someone who has not seen the draft. Ask them what the article is about after they have only scrolled. They should be able to answer from the title and the headings. Then ask them to read one section properly. They should not pinch-zoom. If they pinch-zoom, the body is too small or too faint.

Set these choices as tokens, not as one-off sizes on a single template. A scale for title, heading, body, and caption, with a measure and a line height for each, will keep the next article in the same system. Tailwind can express that scale as a small set of utilities. The point of the scale is that a writer can publish the next piece without inventing a new poster.

When a reading system like this needs to sit inside a whole site, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) and bring one article you wish were easier to finish. The useful review is a person reading, not a font menu.

Pictures are the other half of a long page, and they are often the thing that makes the page slow. [Images that survive a slow connection](/blog/images-that-survive-a-slow-connection) is the next piece, because a comfortable column still fails if the photograph above it never arrives.
